claim: The phylum Apicomplexa groups intracellular parasites that employ substrate-dependent gliding motility to invade host cells, egress from infected cells, and cross biological barriers.
source: The phylum of Apicomplexa groups intracellular parasites that employ substrate-dependent gliding motility to invade host cells, egress from the infected cells, and cross biological barriers.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established knowledge about Apicomplexa parasites.

claim: The glideosome-associated connector (GAC) is a conserved protein essential to gliding motility.
source: The glideosome-associated connector (GAC) is a conserved protein essential to this process.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research and is presented as established knowledge.

claim: GAC facilitates the association of actin filaments with surface transmembrane adhesins.
source: GAC facilitates the association of actin filaments with surface transmembrane adhesins and the efficient transmission of the force generated by myosin translocation of actin to the cell surface substrate.
evidence: This is a functional description of GAC supported by prior research.

claim: The crystal structure of Toxoplasma gondii GAC reveals a unique, supercoiled armadillo repeat region that adopts a closed ring conformation.
source: Here, we present the crystal structure of Toxoplasma gondii GAC and reveal a unique, supercoiled armadillo repeat region that adopts a closed ring conformation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the crystal structure determination presented in this manuscript.

claim: GAC adopts several conformations from closed to open and extended.
source: Characterisation of the solution properties together with membrane and F-actin binding interfaces suggests that GAC adopts several conformations from closed to open and extended.
evidence: This conclusion is based on SAXS, HDX-MS, and other biophysical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular unicellular parasite and a prominent member of the Apicomplexa phylum.
source: Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular unicellular parasite and a prominent member of the Apicomplexa phylum (Kim and Weiss, 2004), which also includes Plasmodium, the causative agent of human malaria (Su et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge about T. gondii supported by citations.

claim: Apicomplexan parasites share a common set of specialised apical organelles, the micronemes and rhoptries, that are critical for invasion.
source: These parasites share a common set of specialised apical organelles, the micronemes and rhoptries, that are critical for invasion (Carruthers and Sibley, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Apicomplexa supported by a citation.

claim: The sequential secretion of micronemes and rhoptries leads to the formation of a moving junction formed between the parasite and host cell plasma membranes.
source: The sequential secretion of both organelles leads to the formation of a moving junction (MJ) formed between the parasite and host cell plasma membranes that participates in active penetration.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of invasion based on established knowledge.

claim: Substrate-dependent, forward parasite propulsion is known as gliding motility and powered by a multiprotein structure referred to as the glideosome.
source: Substrate-dependent, forward parasite propulsion is known as gliding motility and powered by a multiprotein structure referred to as the glideosome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of parasite motility.

claim: A myosin motor comprising myosin A (MyoA), a class XIV myosin heavy chain and its myosin light chains, together with glideosome-associated proteins (GAPs) interact with and generate rearward translocation of actin filaments along the parasite.
source: A myosin motor comprising myosin A (MyoA), a class XIV myosin heavy chain and its myosin light chains, together with glideosome-associated proteins (GAPs) interact with and generate rearward translocation of actin filaments (F-actin) along the parasite (Powell et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the molecular components of the glideosome supported by a citation.

claim: GAC protein is a central bridging component of the gliding machinery.
source: The glideosome-associated connector (GAC) protein is a central bridging component of the gliding machinery (Jacot et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: GAC is a large protein composed of numerous armadillo repeats (ARMs) and is highly conserved throughout the Apicomplexa phylum.
source: This large protein composed of numerous armadillo repeats (ARMs) is highly conserved throughout the Apicomplexa phylum and links F-actin to the TRAP/MIC family of surface adhesins at the plasma membrane, which targets host cell ligands and mediates adherent anchor points.
evidence: This describes the structural features and conservation of GAC based on prior knowledge.

claim: GAC links F-actin to the TRAP/MIC family of surface adhesins at the plasma membrane.
source: This large protein composed of numerous armadillo repeats (ARMs) is highly conserved throughout the Apicomplexa phylum and links F-actin to the TRAP/MIC family of surface adhesins at the plasma membrane, which targets host cell ligands and mediates adherent anchor points.
evidence: This describes the functional role of GAC based on prior knowledge.

claim: TgMIC2 is a key member of the TRAP/MIC family that supports gliding motility and host cell invasion.
source: A key member of the TRAP/MIC family is the transmembrane micronemal protein 2 (TgMIC2) that supports gliding motility and host cell invasion (Huynh and Carruthers, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The ectodomain of TgMIC2 comprises a von Willebrand factor A domain and multiple thrombospondin repeat domains that associate with an accessory protein (M2AP) and host cells.
source: The ectodomain of TgMIC2 comprises a von Willebrand factor A domain and multiple thrombospondin repeat domains that associate with an accessory protein (M2AP) and host cells (Huynh et al., 2015; Jewett and Sibley, 2004; Song and Springer, 2014; Tonkin et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the structural features of TgMIC2 supported by citations.

claim: TgMIC2 is predicted to connect the parasite actomyosin system through an interaction between GAC and its cytoplasmic tail.
source: TgMIC2 is predicted to connect the parasite actomyosin system through an interaction between GAC and its cytoplasmic tail.
evidence: This is a prediction based on prior knowledge and inference.

claim: GAC moves dynamically with the moving junction from the parasite apical to the basal pole during gliding motility, host cell egress, and invasion.
source: GAC moves dynamically with the MJ from the parasite apical to the basal pole during gliding motility, host cell egress, and invasion.
evidence: This describes the dynamic behavior of GAC based on prior observations.

claim: Rearward translocation of adhesins anchored to both the parasite plasma membrane and the host membrane by the inner-membrane-associated glideosome generates parasite forward movement.
source: Rearward translocation of adhesins anchored to both the parasite plasma membrane and the host membrane by the inner-membrane-associated glideosome generates parasite forward movement (Carruthers and Tomley, 2008; Frénal et al., 2017a).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of parasite motility supported by citations.

claim: The initial apical location of GAC depends on the activity of an apical lysine methyltransferase (AKMT), through a yet unknown mechanism.
source: The initial apical location of GAC depends on the activity of an apical lysine methyltransferase (AKMT), through a yet unknown mechanism (Jacot et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ultrastructure expansion microscopy localised GAC and formin 1 (FRM1) to the preconoidal rings (PCRs).
source: Recently ultrastructure expansion microscopy localised GAC and formin 1 (FRM1) to the preconoidal rings (PCRs; Dos Santos Pacheco et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: FRM1 is the only and essential nucleator of actin polymerisation to drive conoid extrusion and parasite motility and invasion.
source: Importantly, FRM1 is the only and essential nucleator of actin polymerisation to drive conoid extrusion and parasite motility and invasion (Tosetti et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The PCRs serve as platform for the assembly of the glideosome.
source: As part of the conoid, the PCRs serve as platform for the assembly of the glideosome.
evidence: This is based on prior knowledge about the conoid structure.

claim: Membrane association of GAC relies on its capacity to bind phosphatidic acid (PA).
source: Membrane association of GAC relies on its capacity to bind phosphatidic acid (PA), an essential lipid mediator for microneme secretion which assists in the correct engagement of GAC (Bullen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PA is an essential lipid mediator for microneme secretion which assists in the correct engagement of GAC.
source: Membrane association of GAC relies on its capacity to bind phosphatidic acid (PA), an essential lipid mediator for microneme secretion which assists in the correct engagement of GAC (Bullen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: An initial small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) model predicted an elongated club-shaped conformation with the C-terminal Pleckstrin homology (PH) domain lying at the extremity of the structure.
source: An initial small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) model predicted an elongated club-shaped conformation with the C-terminal Pleckstrin homology (PH) domain lying at the extremity of the structure (Jacot et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes a prior structural model supported by a citation.

claim: Well-diffracting and reproducible crystals were obtained at pH 5 for native full-length TgGAC (residues 1–2639).
source: Well-diffracting and reproducible crystals were obtained at pH 5 for native full-length TgGAC (residues 1–2639; Kumar et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions for crystallization.

claim: Selenomethionine-substituted crystals produced sufficient anomalous signal for phase determination.
source: Selenomethionine-substituted crystals were also obtained that produced sufficient anomalous signal for phase determination.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for structure determination.

claim: The structure was solved by multiple-wavelength anomalous dispersion (MAD) to 2.7 Å resolution with an Rfree of 26%.
source: The structure was solved by multiple-wavelength anomalous dispersion (MAD) to 2.7 Å resolution with an Rfree of 26% (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the resolution and quality of the crystal structure.

claim: The electron density for residues 7–2504 was of sufficient quality to facilitate modelling for these residues.
source: The electron density for residues 7–2504 was of sufficient quality to facilitate modelling for these residues (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the quality of the electron density map and is supported by figures.

claim: The remaining electron density showed evidence of peptide backbone but could not be confidently modelled and refined, indicating a degree of conformational flexibility for residues 2505–2639.
source: The remaining electron density showed evidence of peptide backbone but could not be confidently modelled and refined, indicating a degree of conformational flexibility for residues 2505–2639.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the electron density data.

claim: Over 80% of the backbone resonances for TgGAC2505–2639 could be confidently assigned using NMR spectroscopy.
source: NMR spectra confirmed an independently folded domain, and over 80% of the backbone resonances could be confidently assigned (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes the NMR assignment results.

claim: The final NMR ensemble for TgGAC2505–2639 was calculated based on 3533 nuclear Overhauser effect and superposes with an average pairwise backbone root mean square deviation (RMSD) of 0.17 Å.
source: The final NMR ensemble was calculated based on 3533 nuclear Overhauser effect and superposes with an average pairwise backbone root mean square deviation (RMSD) of 0.17 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes the quality of the NMR structure.

claim: Excellent agreement is observed between the experimental NMR structure and predicted AlphaFold2 structure for TgGAC2505–2639 with a backbone RMSD of 1.5 Å.
source: Excellent agreement is observed between the experimental NMR structure and predicted from the AlphaFold2 structure with a backbone RMSD of 1.5 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This compares the experimental NMR structure with a computational prediction.

claim: The structure of TgGAC2505–2639 adopts a PH-like domain fold comprising a seven-stranded β-barrel with three α-helices.
source: The structure of TgGAC2505–2639 adopts a PH-like domain fold comprising a seven-stranded β-barrel with three α-helices.
evidence: This describes the structural fold of the PH domain.

claim: The presence of an extended N-terminal-helix is reminiscent of the PH domains from TgAPH and TgISP and appears to be a common feature among apicomplexan PH domains.
source: The presence of an extended N-terminal-helix is reminiscent of the PH domains from TgAPH and TgISP (Darvill et al., 2018; Tonkin et al., 2014) and appears to be a common feature among apicomplexan PH domains.
evidence: This is a comparison with other known structures supported by citations.

claim: The crystal structure of TgGAC7–2504 comprises 169 helices arranged in 53 consecutive helical bundles that resemble ARM and HEAT-like repeats (AHRs) linked to the mixed α/β C-terminal PH domain.
source: The crystal structure of TgGAC7–2504 comprises 169 helices (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2) arranged in 53 consecutive helical bundles that resemble ARM and HEAT-like repeats (AHRs; Kippert and Gerloff, 2009) linked to the mixed α/β C-terminal PH domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the overall architecture of the crystal structure.

claim: The architecture of TgGAC can be divided into three major regions (RI, RII, and RIII).
source: The architecture can be divided into three major regions (RI, RII, and RIII).
evidence: This describes the structural organization of TgGAC.

claim: RI (residues 1–1665) comprises 37 consecutive AHRs of approximately 40 residues long that are supercoiled into a three-layer pyramid structure.
source: RI (residues 1–1665) comprises 37 consecutive AHRs of approximately 40 residues long that are supercoiled into a three-layer pyramid structure (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the structure of region I.

claim: RII comprises 16 canonical armadillo repeats (AHR38-53) and forms a superhelical arch that contacts the base of the RI pyramid helical regions.
source: RII comprises 16 canonical armadillo repeats (AHR38-53) and forms a superhelical arch that contacts the base of the RI pyramid helical regions.
evidence: This describes the structure of region II.

claim: The N/C interface in TgGAC encompasses a surface area of 1550 Å2, with AHR1 and AHR17-18 from RI forming one side while AHR48-50 from RII form the other.
source: This interface encompasses a surface area of 1550 Å2, with AHR1 and AHR17-18 from RI forming one side while AHR48-50 from RII form the other (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the N/C interface based on structural analysis.

claim: The N/C interface comprises several prominent electrostatic interactions (K2254-D11, E2436-H24, D2330-R629, D2346-K672, and D2197-R716).
source: The interface comprises several prominent electrostatic interactions (K2254-D11, E2436-H24, D2330-R629, D2346-K672, and D2197-R716; Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes specific interactions at the N/C interface.

claim: AHR50 has a large helix-loop-helix insertion (residues 2278–2337) between the second and third helices which creates a prominent protrusion that stabilises the interface.
source: AHR50 also has a large helix-loop-helix insertion (residues 2278–2337) between the second and third helices which creates a prominent protrusion that also stabilises the interface (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This describes a structural feature of AHR50.

claim: Residues forming key features of the TgGAC structure are highly conserved across GAC orthologues in Apicomplexa.
source: Residues forming these key features of the structure are highly conserved across GAC orthologues in Apicomplexa (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The closed conformation observed in the TgGAC crystal structure deviates significantly from the extended club-shaped structure that was proposed from previous SAXS analyses.
source: The closed conformation observed in the TgGAC crystal structure deviates significantly from the extended club-shaped structure that was proposed from previous SAXS analyses (Jacot et al., 2016), which raises concern that it could be an artefact of crystallisation.
evidence: This compares the current structure with a prior model.

claim: The overall architecture of the AlphaFold2 predicted structures for TgGAC and PfGAC is very similar to that observed in the crystal structure of TgGAC.
source: Remarkably, the overall architecture of the predicted structures is very similar to that observed in the crystal structure of TgGAC (Figure 2A), as it is characterised by a series of tandem AHRs that are supercoiled into a large ring and is closed by specific interactions between N- and C-terminal AHRs.
evidence: This compares the crystal structure with computational predictions.

claim: The N-/C-terminal interface that characterises the closed structure is conserved at the amino acid sequence level.
source: The N-/C-terminal interface that characterises the closed structure is conserved at the amino acid sequence level (Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: At pH 8.0, masses of 264 kDa (Guiner) and 286 kDa (IFT) were obtained for TgGAC, which are close to the expected value of 286 kDa for a TgGAC monomer.
source: At pH 8.0, masses of 264 kDa (Guiner) and 286 kDa (IFT) were obtained, which are close to the expected value of 286 kDa for a TgGAC monomer.
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis.

claim: The radius of gyration (Rg) values of 105 Å and 122 Å for TgGAC at pH 8.0 are much larger than the Rg of 48 Å calculated from the crystal structure.
source: The radius of gyration, Rg, values of, respectively, 105 Å and 122 Å were obtained, which are much larger than the Rg of 48 Å calculated from the crystal structure of TgGAC.
evidence: This compares SAXS data with the crystal structure.

claim: The maximum intramolecular distances for TgGAC are 394 Å from SAXS data and 138 Å from the crystal structure.
source: This discrepancy in size is also clearly seen when comparing the p(r) function calculated from the SAXS data and the crystal structure, where the maximum intramolecular distances are 394 Å and 138 Å, respectively (Figure 2C).
evidence: This compares SAXS data with the crystal structure.

claim: TgGAC is primarily a monomer in solution at pH 8.0 but forms a much more extended structure than seen in the crystal structure whilst maintaining key structural elements.
source: Overall, the data and the models show that even though TgGAC is primarily a monomer in solution at pH 8.0, it forms a much more extended structure than seen in the crystal structure whilst maintaining key structural elements.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on SAXS and modeling data.

claim: A closed structure is likely to be an important stable functional state as the N-/C-interface is encoded within the sequence conservation.
source: Collectively, it can be concluded that a closed structure is likely to be an important stable functional state as the N-/C-interface is encoded within the sequence conservation.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation and structural data.

claim: The extended, flexible structures observed in solution may play a role in facilitating the assembly GAC with its binding partners.
source: The extended, flexible structures observed in solution may play a role is a facilitating the assembly GAC with its binding partners.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed structural flexibility.

claim: An extended patch of conserved basic residues is formed on one face of the PH domain in GAC which is reminiscent of the charge distribution on TgAPH, suggesting a similar role in phospholipid binding.
source: An extended patch of conserved basic residues is formed on one face of the PH domain in GAC which is reminiscent of the charge distribution on TgAPH (Darvill et al., 2018), suggesting a similar role in phospholipid binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison with TgAPH.

claim: Both PfGAC and TgGAC bind specifically to PA as demonstrated by phospholipid strip assays.
source: Using phospholipid strip assays, it had been previously demonstrated that both PfGAC and TgGAC bind specifically to PA (Jacot et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In all three CG-MD simulation repeats, GAC bound to the membrane within 10 μs.
source: In all three simulation repeats, GAC bound to the membrane within 10 μs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Analysis of protein-lipid contacts highlighted two key membrane-bound regions in GAC, which localised to the PH domain and an adjacent basic protrusion from AHR53.
source: Analysis of protein-lipid contacts highlighted two key membrane-bound regions, which localised to the PH domain and an adjacent basic protrusion from AHR53 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The Kdapp for PfGACPH binding LUVs composed of 50% POPA was calculated to be 60±3 μM.
source: The Kdapp for PfGACPH binding LUVs composed of 50% POPA was calculated to be 60±3 μM.
evidence: This is based on NMR titration experiments.

claim: PREs mapped onto the structure of PfGACPH reveal a contiguous surface formed from residues located within the β1-strand, bordering the β1–β2 loop, within the β5–β6 loop and the loop region between β7 strand and C-terminal α-helix.
source: PREs mapped onto the structure of PfGACPH reveal a contiguous surface formed from residues located within the β1-strand, bordering the β1–β2 loop, within the β5–β6 loop and the loop region between β7 strand and C-terminal α-helix (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on NMR PRE data.

claim: A comparative analysis of the PH binding residues compared to simulation with full-length TgGAC indicated that the PH domain alone binds with the same interface in the context of the whole GAC protein.
source: A comparative analysis of the PH binding residues compared to simulation with full-length TgGAC indicated that the PH domain alone binds with the same interface in the context of the whole GAC protein (Figure 4F).
evidence: This compares NMR data with molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: NMR titrations performed with TgGACPH and PA-enriched paramagnetic nanodiscs confirmed an identical PA-binding surface to PfGAC.
source: NMR titrations performed with TgGACPH and PA-enriched paramagnetic nanodiscs confirmed an identical PA-binding surface to PfGAC (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on NMR titration experiments.

claim: Mutation of basic residues in PfGACPH reduced the affinity for PA-enriched MSP1E1 nanodiscs, indicating that these residues are important for binding PA within a membrane environment.
source: Compared to WT (Kdapp of 270±40 μM), mutation of basic residues reduced the affinity for PA-enriched MSP1E1 nanodiscs, indicating that these residues are important for binding PA within a membrane environment (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on NMR binding assays with mutant proteins.

claim: All three mutant proteins tested exhibited a significant reduction in binding to PA enriched liposomes.
source: All mutant proteins tested exhibited a significant reduction in binding to PA enriched liposomes (Figure 5B and C), with the most dramatic effects observed for the triple mutant KER2619–2621AAA and paired in quintuple mutant RK2587–88AA/KER2619–2621AAA.
evidence: This is based on liposome binding assays.

claim: All GAC versions, wild-type, mutated and chimeric, localised correctly at the PCRs of the parasite as well as cytosolically, suggesting that the PA-binding by the GAC PH domain is not critical for GACs apical localisation.
source: All GAC versions, wild-type, mutated and chimeric, localised correctly at the PCRs of the parasite as well as cytosolically (Figure 6A), suggesting that the PA-binding by the GAC PH domain is not critical for GACs apical localisation.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence assays in parasites.

claim: Upon triggering parasite motility with BIPPO, all the strains displayed the characteristic basal accumulation of TgGAC.
source: Likewise, upon triggering parasite motility with 5-Benzyl-3-isopropyl-1H-pyrazolo[4,3-d]pyrimidin-7(6H)-one (BIPPO), all the strains displayed the characteristic basal accumulation of TgGAC (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence assays in parasites.

claim: The mutations in the PA-binding site of GAC were not detrimental for the parasite lytic cycle.
source: Finally, to access if there was any fitness cost induced by the mutations, wild-type, and mutated parasites were analysed by plaque assay and revealed that the mutations were not detrimental for the parasite lytic cycle (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on plaque assays.

claim: No clear defect in invasion could be observed in parasites expressing the mutated versions of GAC.
source: Accordingly, no clear defect in invasion could be observed in parasites expressing the mutated versions (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on invasion assays.

claim: A small reduction of the plaque size and reduction in invasion capacity was observed for the TgGAC-PfPH chimera.
source: A small reduction of the plaque size and reduction in invasion capacity was observed for the TgGAC-PfPH chimera.
evidence: This is based on plaque and invasion assays.

claim: Association to rabbit F-actin was previously shown to involve the N-terminal 1114 amino acids of TgGAC, roughly corresponding to the first 25 AHRs of the RI region.
source: Association to rabbit F-actin was previously shown to involve the N-terminal 1114 amino acids of TgGAC, roughly corresponding to the first 25 AHRs of the RI region (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is based on prior work.

claim: Both full-length TgGAC and a fragment encompassing residues GAC1–1114 co-sedimented with Toxoplasma F-actin produced from recombinant TgACT.
source: Both full-length TgGAC and a fragment encompassing residues GAC1–1114 co-sedimented with Toxoplasma F-actin produced from recombinant TgACT (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is based on co-sedimentation assays.

claim: A shorter N-terminal fragment, (TgGAC1–619) corresponding to the first 14 AHRs, failed to interact with F-actin.
source: In contrast, a shorter N-terminal fragment, (TgGAC1–619) corresponding to the first 14 AHRs, failed to interact with F-actin.
evidence: This is based on co-sedimentation assays.

claim: Either the binding site for F-actin lies between residues 619 and 1114 of TgGAC or the isolated N-terminal fragment TgGAC1–619 adopts a different conformation than TgGAC1–1114 and TgGAC which prevents its interaction with F-actin.
source: This suggests that either the binding site for F-actin lies between residues 619 and 1114 of TgGAC or that that isolated N-terminal fragment TgGAC1–619 adopts a different conformation than TgGAC1–1114 and TgGAC which prevents its interaction with F-actin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding data.

claim: Most of the GAC N-terminus exhibited identical dynamics in all constructs (TgGAC1–619, TgGAC1–1114, and TgGAC-FL) as measured by HDX-MS.
source: Most of the GAC N-terminus exhibited identical dynamics in all constructs (Figure 7F and G), and only the C-terminal extremity of TgGAC1–619 (residues 559–609) displayed higher H/D exchange rate compared to TgGAC1–1114 and TgGAC-FL (Figure 7F–I).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS data.

claim: Only the C-terminal extremity of TgGAC1–619 (residues 559–609) displayed higher H/D exchange rate compared to TgGAC1–1114 and TgGAC-FL.
source: Most of the GAC N-terminus exhibited identical dynamics in all constructs (Figure 7F and G), and only the C-terminal extremity of TgGAC1–619 (residues 559–609) displayed higher H/D exchange rate compared to TgGAC1–1114 and TgGAC-FL (Figure 7F–I).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS data.

claim: TgGAC1–1114 and TgGAC-FL share identical dynamics within the region 559-609.
source: TgGAC1–1114 and TgGAC-FL share identical dynamics within this region.
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS data.

claim: The two truncated fragments (TgGAC1–619 and TgGAC1–1114) share a similar conformation as TgGAC-FL for residues 1–558, corresponding to a major portion (14 AHRs) of the first turn in the superhelical pyramid structure (19 AHRs).
source: This indicates that the two truncated fragments share a similar conformation as TgGAC-FL for residues 1–558, corresponding to a major portion (14 AHRs) of the first turn in the superhelical pyramid structure (19 AHRs).
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data.

claim: The C-terminal extremity of the shortest fragment, TgGAC1–619, is significantly more flexible which also may contribute to its inability to bind F-actin.
source: The C-terminal extremity of the shortest fragment, TgGAC1–619, is significantly more flexible which also may contribute to its inability to bind F-actin.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data and binding assays.

claim: The most striking feature of the TgGAC structure is the large continuous supercoiled ARM region (residues 1–2490) which forms a ring.
source: The most striking feature of the TgGAC structure is the large continuous supercoiled ARM region (residues 1–2490) which forms a ring.
evidence: This is a description of the crystal structure.

claim: The closure of the ring results from an extensive interface between the ARM1 and ARMs14-16 from RI and ARMs46-48 from RII (N/C-interface).
source: The closure of the ring results from an extensive interface between the ARM1 and ARMs14-16 from RI and ARMs46-48 from RII (N/C-interface - Figure 2).
evidence: This is a description of the crystal structure.

claim: The nature of the N/C interface in the closed structure is hydrophilic with several electrostatic interactions, including some that are readily titratable, such H24 and H2164.
source: The nature of the N/C interface in the closed structure is hydrophilic with several electrostatic interactions, including some that are readily titratable, such H24 and H2164.
evidence: This is a description of the crystal structure.

claim: Deprotonation of titratable residues at high pH may remove key salt bridges that stabilise the closed conformation and facilitate a conformationally labile open structure.
source: It is conceivable that deprotonation of these residues at high pH removes key salt bridges that stabilise the closed conformation and facilitate a conformationally labile open structure.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural features and SAXS data.

claim: The ability of GAC to adopt both a flexible open conformation and transition to a closed ring structure could play a role in regulating the multiple interactions of GAC assembly on the glideosome and to the parasite membrane.
source: The ability of GAC to adopt both a flexible open conformation and transition to a closed ring structure could play a role in regulating the multiple interactions of GAC assembly on the glideosome and to the parasite membrane.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural data.

claim: This behaviour is reminiscent of the unrelated ARM-rich protein, HUWE1, which is a quality-control E3 ligase, which forms a large, closed ring from 34 tandem ARM repeats.
source: This behaviour is reminiscent of the unrelated ARM-rich protein, HUWE1, which is a quality-control E3 ligase, which forms a large, closed ring from 34 tandem ARM repeats.
evidence: This is a comparison with another protein supported by a citation.

claim: The closed structure of HUWE1 is believed to represent a latent state but can adopt a range of open conformations to regulate its interactions with accessory proteins.
source: The closed structure is believed to represent a latent state but can adopt a range of open conformations to regulate its interactions with accessory proteins (Grabarczyk et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: GAC interacts with PA-enriched membranes that are generated through a signalling cascade in activated parasites.
source: GAC interacts with PA-enriched membranes that are generated through a signalling cascade in activated parasites (Bullen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Other regions in GAC, such as the basic protrusion in AHR53, are also likely to contribute to membrane binding in vivo.
source: Other regions in GAC, such as the basic protrusion in AHR53 (Figure 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), are also likely to contribute to membrane binding in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and simulation data.

claim: The presence of a membrane interaction surface within the TgGACPH suggests that the binding site for the juxtamembrane region of the MIC2 cytoplasmic tail is located nearby, and these interactions may also be cooperative.
source: Furthermore, the presence of a membrane interaction surface within the TgGACPH suggests that the binding site for the juxtamembrane region of the MIC2 cytoplasmic tail is located nearby, and these interactions may also be cooperative.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural data.

claim: The principal Toxoplasma F-actin binding region is localised to the first 1114 residues of TgGAC (TgGAC1–1114), which forms a large, supercoiled base of the N-terminal pyramid (TgGAC-R1:1–1656) and provides a platform with several potential sites of interaction with a helical actin filament.
source: The principal Toxoplasma F-actin binding region is localised to the first 1114 residues of TgGAC (TgGAC1–1114), which forms a large, supercoiled base of the N-terminal pyramid (TgGAC-R1:1–1656 – Figure 2) and provides a platform with several potential sites of interaction with a helical actin filament.
evidence: This is based on binding assays and structural analysis.

claim: The minimal actin-binding interface lies between residues 559–1114 (AHRs 15–25) in which the second supercoiled turn starts.
source: Analysis of the protein conformation by HDX-MS showed that TgGAC1–619 adopts a similar conformation for residues 1–558 as in full-length TgGAC, suggesting that the minimal actin-binding interface lies between residues 559–1114 (AHRs 15–25) in which the second supercoiled turn starts.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS and binding data.

claim: The absence of F-actin binding for the N-terminal portion (1–619), which forms the base of GAC pyramidal structure, suggests a role in this region in stabilising the closed conformation as it makes direct contact with the C-terminal end of the RII region.
source: The absence of F-actin binding for the N-terminal portion (1–619), which forms the base of GAC pyramidal structure, suggests a role in this region in stabilising the closed conformation as it makes direct contact with the C-terminal end of the RII region.
evidence: This is an inference based on binding data and structural analysis.

claim: Membrane association simulations for TgGAC reveal a specific membrane-binding surface involving the PH domain and RII, and this orientation places the TgGAC1–1114 region distal for interaction with the actin filament.
source: Membrane association simulations for TgGAC reveal a specific membrane-binding surface involving the PH domain and RII, and this orientation places the TgGAC1–1114 region distal for interaction with the actin filament.
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The closed structure is likely to represent a functional important state of cytosolic GAC or during GACs initial engagement within the glideosome.
source: As the available pellicular space between the parasite inner membrane complex and the plasma membrane is insufficient for the open structure of GAC (i.e. with RII and RIII extended) to bridge F-actin to the plasma membrane lengthways, the closed structure is likely to represent a functional important state of cytosolic GAC or during GACs initial engagement within the glideosome.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and spatial constraints.

claim: PA binding and MIC2 recruitment at the plasma membrane by GAC may contribute to conformational changes to GAC structure, i.e., a transition from closed to open and extended structures.
source: It is therefore conceivable that PA binding and MIC2 recruitment at the plasma membrane by GAC contribute to conformational changes to GAC structure, i.e., a transition from closed to open and extended structures.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural data and comparison with ERM proteins.

claim: The C-terminal AHR arch region (AHRs 38–53) displays significant structural similarity with the armadillo repeat region (ARM) of the ß-catenins, superimposing with an RMSD of 4.2 Å over the backbone of 348 equivalent residues.
source: The C-terminal AHR arch region (AHRs 38–53) displays significant structural similarity with the armadillo repeat region (ARM) of the ß-catenins, superimposing with an RMSD of 4.2 Å over the backbone of 348 equivalent residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The single chain of GAC carries out both the roles of α-catenin and β-catenin, i.e., RI acts like the actin-binding α-catenin and is linked via L1 to RII ARM arch structure, which like β-catenin tethers the system to the cell surface adhesins.
source: The single chain of GAC carries out both these roles, i.e., RI acts like the actin-binding α-catenin and is linked via L1 to RII ARM arch structure, which like β-catenin tethers the system to the cell surface adhesins.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison with catenins.

claim: It is tempting to speculate that a similar interface formed in ß-catenin/E-cadherin complexes is used by TgGAC to link TgMIC2 to the glideosome machinery.
source: As TgGAC likely binds the cytoplasmic C-terminal tails of the plasma membrane adhesin TgMIC2 (Jacot et al., 2016), it is tempting to speculate that a similar interface formed in ß-catenin/E-cadherin complexes is used by TgGAC to link TgMIC2 to the glideosome machinery (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural similarity.

claim: Mechanical force induces a rearrangement of binding interfaces in catenins that result in a strengthening of its interaction with F-actin, and this effect is dependent on the direction of applied force.
source: Mechanical force induces a rearrangement of binding interfaces that result in a strengthening of its interaction with F-actin, and this effect is dependent on the direction of applied force (Mei et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Part of the 559–1114 F-actin binding region is not fully accessible in the closed conformation; therefore, it is conceivable that optimal F-actin binding requires significant structural rearrangement of the closed structure.
source: Importantly, part of the 559–1114 F-actin binding region is not fully accessible in the closed conformation; therefore, it is also conceivable that optimal F-actin binding requires significant structural rearrangement of the closed structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: The stabilised closed conformation would be able to both resist and sense the significant inter parasite–substrate forces generated by MyoA translocation of F-actin.
source: The stabilised closed conformation would be able to both resist and sense the significant inter parasite–substrate forces generated by MyoA translocation of F-actin.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural features.

claim: Force acting along parasite–host cell interface could induce opening of the GAC structure and unveil additional cryptic binding sites that strengthen F-actin binding and ensure a coordinated direction of motion.
source: Such force acting along parasite–host cell interface could induce opening of the GAC structure and unveil additional cryptic binding sites that strengthen F-actin binding and ensure a coordinated direction of motion.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural features and comparison with catenins.

claim: The lower affinity of full-length TgGAC compared to TgGAC1–1114 for F-actin supports the hypothesis that optimal F-actin binding requires structural rearrangement.
source: The lower affinity of full-length TgGAC compared to TgGAC1–1114 for F-actin supports this hypothesis (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on binding assay data.

claim: Structural similarity exists between the C-terminal ARM region of GAC (TgGAC1670–2639) and the family of myosin-specific chaperones which possess ARM-rich UCS (UNC-45/Cro1/She4) domains.
source: Structural similarity also exists between the C-terminal ARM region of GAC (TgGAC1670–2639) and the family of myosin-specific chaperones which possess ARM-rich UCS (UNC-45/Cro1/She4) domains (Hellerschmied and Clausen, 2014) that interact with myosin motors domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison supported by a citation.

claim: T. gondii possesses a dedicated UCS chaperone for TgMyoA (TgUNC), which is critical for successful folding of all the parasite myosin motors.
source: While T. gondii possesses a dedicated UCS chaperone for TgMyoA (TgUNC; Bookwalter et al., 2014), which is critical for successful folding of all the parasite myosin motors (Frénal et al., 2017b), the similarity between the GAC C-terminal ARM region and the UCS chaperones is intriguing.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: It is tempting to speculate that TgGAC may assist TgMyoA organisation on F-actin.
source: Although no direct evidence for an interaction between TgGAC and TgMyoA has been found, it is tempting to speculate that TgGAC may assist TgMyoA organisation on F-actin.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural similarity.
